printed_headline_estimate: Binary logistic regression predicting Improved Toilet (NFHS-4 2014-15, N not reported; Table 2, PDF p. 3 / p. 219): Poorest B = -5.383, Sig. = 0.000, Exp(B) = 0.005; Poorer B = -3.783, Sig. = 0.000, Exp(B) = 0.023; Middle B = -2.715, Sig. = 0.000, Exp(B) = 0.066; Richer B = -1.151, Sig. = 0.000, Exp(B) = 0.221; Urban B = -0.156, Sig. = 0.000, Exp(B) = 0.855; Intercept B = 1.954, Sig. = 0.000 (tested predictors are demographic/socioeconomic wealth quintiles and urban locality only; no legal/institutional exposure tested).
publication_year_note: Printed as 2021 in Problemy Ekorozwoju – Problems of Sustainable Development, Vol. 16, No. 2, pp. 217-225 (DOI: 10.35784/pe.2021.2.23); no separate online-first date printed.
rationale: The paper reports one inferential quantitative analysis—a binary logistic regression using NFHS-4 (2014-15) data predicting household access to an improved toilet facility (Table 2, p. 219)—alongside descriptive NFHS-4 percentages (Figure 1, Table 1) and Scopus publication counts (Figure 2). However, the tested independent variables in the logistic regression are strictly socioeconomic and demographic (household Wealth Index quintiles: Poorest, Poorer, Middle, Richer; and Urban vs. rural locality). All discussion of legal, administrative, financial, and governance mechanisms (e.g., government manual verification rules for subsidies, Output Based Aid, SHGs, PPPs, the Prohibition of Defecation in Open Places Bill 2019, and Gram Panchayat rules) is purely qualitative and narrative. Thus, the tested quantitative exposure-outcome pair fails narrow Criterion 2 and has no SWiM-eligible effect.
